pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Conduction, convection, and radiation

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 Physics, 'Energy: Energy changes and transfers' — statutory wording: 'Heating and thermal equilibrium: temperature difference between 2 objects leading to energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler one, through contact (conduction) or radiation; such transfers tending to reduce the temperature difference; use of insulators' (verified by fetch). NOTE — the KS3 statutory statement names ONLY conduction and radiation; CONVECTION is not named in this Energy statement, though it is conventionally taught and is supported by the KS3 'Matter / Energy in matter' content ('changes with temperature in motion and spacing of particles').

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** MS-PS3 Energy — MS-PS3-3 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3]' (insulated box / solar cooker / Styrofoam cup), underpinned by DCI PS3.A 'Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of matter' and PS3.B 'Energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions or objects and into colder ones' (verified by fetch). Both tiers place this content at lower-secondary / middle school and qualitative; quantitative heat-transfer is deferred (KS4 / HS).

- **Operational details:** This topic asks them to use particles to EXPLAIN three distinct mechanisms qualitatively — no equations yet. The organising idea is that a TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE drives energy from hotter to cooler until the difference is gone (thermal equilibrium), and the three mechanisms are three different WAYS that happens: conduction (energy passed along by vibrating/colliding particles, fastest in metals via free electrons — the material does NOT move), convection (the heated FLUID itself becomes less dense, rises, and circulates — the material moves in a loop), and radiation (infrared emitted across empty space, needing no particles at all). The single most important teaching move is to make the child say WHAT is moving in each case (energy along stationary particles vs. the bulk fluid vs. an EM wave), because almost every misconception comes from blurring those. Pair each mechanism with its canonical particle picture and a real example, and tie rate to temperature difference.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ~12–13). The child already has the particle model and the energy stores/pathways framework (prereqs).
bestPractices: Frame everything under ONE rule first — energy moves from hotter to cooler until the temperature difference disappears (thermal equilibrium) — then present the three mechanisms as three different ways that rule is carried out.

For EACH mechanism, make the child state explicitly WHAT moves: conduction = energy passed along by particles that stay put; convection = the heated fluid itself physically circulates; radiation = an infrared wave crosses a gap with no particles needed. This single distinction pre-empts most errors.

Use particle diagrams as the backbone: vibrating, fixed particles handing energy to neighbours (conduction, with free electrons drawn in metals to explain why metals are fast); a convection loop showing warmed fluid expanding, rising, cooling, sinking; radiation as wavy IR arrows across empty space.

Confront the 'cold flows in' idea head-on with the hotter-to-cooler rule: cold is not a substance that travels; a cold object simply gains energy and the warm one loses it. Use a draught / ice example and ask 'is cold coming in, or is warmth leaving?'

Use the metal-vs-wood 'feel' demonstration: two objects at the SAME room temperature feel different because metal conducts energy away from your warm hand faster — separating temperature from rate of conduction, and feeling from temperature.

Teach radiation as universal: ALL objects emit and absorb infrared (not just hot or 'dangerous' things); use thermal-imaging examples and the matt-black-vs-shiny surface result (dark, dull surfaces are better emitters and absorbers).

Link rate to temperature difference quantitatively-in-words: a bigger temperature difference means a faster transfer, and the rate falls as the difference shrinks — connect to why a hot drink cools fast at first then slowly.

Sort everyday examples by mechanism and by 'what moves' (radiator warms a room mostly by convection despite its name; the Sun reaches us by radiation through empty space; a metal spoon in soup by conduction) to force application of the model.
keyRepresentations: Particle diagram of conduction — a row of fixed, vibrating particles passing energy along to neighbours; free electrons added for metals to show why metals conduct fastest.

Convection-current loop — a cross-section (beaker or room) with arrows showing warmed fluid expanding, becoming less dense, rising, cooling and sinking; the MATERIAL circulates, the heat does not 'pass through' stationary fluid.
Infrared radiation arrows across a gap / vacuum — wavy IR emitted and absorbed with no medium; thermal-imaging (false-colour) photos.
The metal-vs-wood 'same temperature, different feel' demo — separating temperature from rate of conduction and from sensation.
Leslie cube / surface-colour comparison — matt black vs shiny silver faces emitting/absorbing IR at different rates.
A temperature-difference → rate dial: bigger difference = faster transfer; the cooling curve that steepens with a larger gap and flattens as equilibrium nears.
commonMisconceptions: 'Cold flows / cold gets in' — treating cold as a substance that travels. Energy only ever moves from hotter to cooler; a cold object gains energy, it does not emit cold.
'Heat rises' — over-generalised. It is warmed FLUID (less dense air/water) that rises in convection; heat itself has no inherent upward direction, and conduction/radiation are not 'up'.
Confusing temperature with heat / thermal energy — temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; a large warm object can hold more thermal energy than a small hot one.
'Metal is colder than wood' — objects in the same room are at the same temperature; metal merely conducts energy away from the hand faster, so it FEELS colder.
'Convection is heat moving through the liquid/gas' — in convection the fluid itself physically circulates; the energy is carried by moving matter, not passed through stationary matter.
'Radiation means nuclear / is only from very hot or dangerous things' — all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation at all times; it needs no medium and is not inherently harmful.
'Wool / a blanket / a coat gives out heat or warms things up' — insulators slow energy transfer; they do not generate heat (a blanket round ice keeps it cold).
Believing the rate of transfer is constant — it depends on the temperature difference, so a hot object cools quickly at first and ever more slowly as it nears equilibrium.
Assuming metals are the only conductors / that 'good conductor' and 'gets hot easily' are the same — conduction is about how fast energy passes through, not how hot a thing gets.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–13 explain conduction, convection and radiation qualitatively using the particle model, organised under one rule: a temperature difference drives energy from hotter to cooler until the difference disappears (thermal equilibrium). The central move is making the learner state explicitly WHAT moves in each case — energy handed along particles that vibrate about fixed positions (conduction), the bulk fluid physically circulating (convection), and an infrared wave that needs no medium and can cross even a vacuum (radiation) — and tying the rate of transfer to the size of the temperature difference. Activities span an interactive particle sandbox, a sorting/assessment check, a reference triptych, a Socratic misconception dialogue, and a spatial loop view, each with a distinct purpose.

activities.title: Particle-level heat sandbox: what is moving in each mechanism?
feedback: If the learner says 'the heat travels up through the water', point to the dyed blob of actual water rising and ask what is moving — the matter or the heat.

When the learner predicts the vacuum will stop radiation, run the toggle: the IR arrows still cross, so this mechanism needs no particles (the perfect vacuum is an idealised model of 'no medium', not an achievable classroom condition).

If the learner calls metal 'colder', show the feel panel with metal and wood at equal temperature, both cooler than the hand, and reframe: the metal conducts energy away from the hand faster, so the hand cools faster.
Prompt the learner to connect the cooling curve that is steep at first and then flattens to a hot drink cooling fast at first and slowly later as the temperature gap shrinks.
On the Leslie cube / surface comparison, reinforce that dull, dark (matt-black) surfaces are better emitters and absorbers of infrared than shiny ones.
activities.rationale: The whole difficulty of this three-mechanism comparison is 'what is moving?'. Live particle motion lets a learner set a temperature difference, watch the rate respond, and see the key dissociations (stationary particles passing energy vs. circulating fluid vs. a wave crossing a vacuum) directly rather than being told. A fixed diagram can name these but cannot be manipulated to show the motion or the rate responding, so dynamic manipulation is proposed here for that specific affordance; efficacy is not independently tested.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: In a conduction mode, heat one end of a bar of fixed, jiggling particles and watch vibration energy pass along to neighbours; toggle 'metal' to add free electrons that carry energy far faster and compare how quickly the far end of a metal vs wooden bar warms.

In a convection mode, heat the bottom of a beaker or room of free fluid particles; follow a dyed blob or arrows as warmed fluid expands (its particles move further apart), becomes less dense and rises, then cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks, tracing a visible loop — then state in words whether the fluid itself moves or the heat passes through still fluid.

In a radiation mode, emit infrared arrows from a hot object across a gap, then use a 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle (an idealised model) and check whether the target still warms; compare a matt-black vs shiny target (the same surface types compared on a Leslie cube, which is usually used to show emission) and see that the matt-black target absorbs infrared faster.
Move one shared 'temperature difference' slider across all three modes and describe how the transfer rate changes as the gap widens and as the two sides drift toward equilibrium.

Use a side 'feel' panel: when metal and wood are at the SAME temperature and both are cooler than the hand, the hand loses warmth faster to the metal — put into words how sensation, temperature and rate differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Each mechanism is a different way the hotter-to-cooler rule is carried out, distinguished by what actually moves: energy along stationary particles, the circulating bulk fluid, or an EM wave needing no medium; transfer rate grows with the temperature difference and falls toward equilibrium.

activities.title: Sort and challenge: which mechanism, and what moves?
feedback: For 'cold coming in', reinforce that cold is not a substance that travels; the warmer food loses energy to the colder freezer interior (and energy from the warmer room leaks into the freezer, not out of it).

For the metal-vs-wood item, use the approximately equal thermometer readings to restate that both are at about the same room temperature, cooler than the hand, and metal simply conducts energy from the hand faster, so it feels colder.
If the radiator is sorted as conduction by its name, note it warms a room mostly by convection despite the name.
activities.rationale: Once the mechanisms are taught, sorting by mechanism and by 'what moves', the predict-and-measure thermometer check, and targeted items on the named misconceptions make a well-defined check that targets errors directly. This is a consolidation/assessment step, not a first encounter; a sort can check classification but recognition-style items do not by themselves elicit independent construction of explanations.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: Drag everyday examples into conduction / convection / radiation: metal spoon in soup, Sun warming skin, hot-air balloon, radiator warming a room, sea breeze — and for each state what is moving.

Predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) reads on a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have sat in the same room long enough to reach room temperature, then measure to check: the readings should be approximately the same, within measurement error.
Answer: 'Food in a freezer gets colder — is cold going into the food, or is energy leaving the food?' and justify using the hotter-to-cooler rule.
Explain why the metal spoon feels colder than the wooden one even though the measurements show approximately equal temperatures (both cooler than your hand).
Complete: 'energy travels from ___ to ___ until the temperature difference is ___'.
Order a cooling drink's transfer rate from fast to slow as the temperature gap shrinks.
activities.intendedInsight: The mechanism distinctions and the hotter-to-cooler rule can be applied to novel everyday cases; approximately equal readings show both spoons are at about the same (room) temperature, and the common cold-flows / heat-rises / metal-is-colder errors can be caught and corrected.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three mechanisms on tap
feedback: Where a learner is unsure which mechanism a situation uses, direct them back to the 'what moves' label for that panel.
Reinforce that all objects emit and absorb infrared, and that matt-black surfaces are better emitters and absorbers than shiny ones.
activities.rationale: A static labelled triptych names the mechanisms and surfaces facts and examples, which is useful for vocabulary and reference. It cannot be manipulated to show particles passing energy, fluid circulating, or rate responding, so it supports rather than carries the core 'what moves' insight and is best paired with the sandbox.
learnerActions: Open three labelled panels (conduction / convection / radiation) and tap a region in each to reveal 'what moves' and a real example.
Use a flap that contrasts shiny vs matt surfaces (as on a Leslie cube) for emitting and absorbing infrared.
Return to this glossary while working in the sandbox to check a term or example.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary, canonical pictures and real examples for each mechanism can be recalled and used as a reference layer.

activities.title: Thermal-imaging engineer: predict and justify
feedback: When the learner attributes feeling to the object's temperature, ask them to separate the object's temperature from the rate and direction energy leaves or enters the hand.

For the hot-railing counterexample, point out the railing is now hotter than the hand, so energy flows railing→hand quickly through the good conductor — fast conduction explains 'feels hot' just as it explained 'feels cold' when the metal was cooler than the hand.
When 'heat rises' appears, prompt for density: the heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks.
If the learner says the duvet 'gives out heat', reframe: insulators only slow energy transfer; a duvet around ice keeps it cold.
activities.rationale: Socratic dialogue is well suited to eliciting and challenging misconceptions by asking the learner to predict and justify. The payoff in this topic is largely visual and dynamic, so dialogue complements the sandbox as a misconception-eliciting warm-up or debrief rather than conveying the motion itself.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role engineer who asks for predictions and reasons: 'Will the vacuum stop the heat? Why?', 'Why does the metal feel colder?', 'You said cold gets in — what is actually moving?'

Tackle the engineer's counterexample: on a hot day a metal railing (hotter than your hand) feels HOT, not cold — explain why the same good conductor now feels hot, separating the object's temperature from the DIRECTION energy flows.
State and defend a prediction, then revise the explanation in terms of what moves after seeing or reasoning through the outcome.
Trace how conduction, convection and radiation each play a part in a radiator heating a room.
Explain why a duvet keeps you warm even though it produces no heat of its own.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending predictions out loud surfaces the stubborn errors (cold flows in, metal is colder, radiation needs a medium, insulators give out heat) so they can be reframed around what actually moves and in which direction energy flows.

activities.title: Spatial convection loop and radiant spread
feedback: If orientation is confusing, return to the 2D cross-section where the loop direction is clearer.
Reinforce that in convection the circulating fluid carries the energy with it; this is much faster than energy passing slowly through still fluid by conduction.
activities.rationale: A spatial view adds a little for the convection loop and radiant spread, which are genuinely three-dimensional. The canonical classroom representations are 2D cross-sections and particle rows, which convey the core 'what moves' idea clearly, so the spatial version is an optional enrichment rather than the primary vehicle.
learnerActions: Explore a room-scale convection loop you can orbit, following warmed, less-dense fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking.
Watch radiant infrared spreading outward from a source through space.
Compare this spatial view with the 2D cross-section and describe what each makes clearer.
activities.intendedInsight: Convection has a genuinely spatial circulating loop and radiation spreads outward in space; seeing this at room scale can make the circulation and spread feel natural.

constraints: KS3 (DfE) statutory Energy wording names only conduction and radiation; convection is conventionally taught and is supported by the KS3 Matter / Energy in matter content on particle motion and spacing changing with temperature — present convection as curriculum-supported but note it is not in the Energy statement.
Keep the treatment qualitative with no equations; quantitative heat-transfer is deferred to KS4 / HS. Tie rate to temperature difference in words, not formulae.
Prerequisites: learners should already have the particle model and the energy stores/pathways framework.

The sorting/quiz check is a consolidation and recognition step; it can check classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of explanations, so pair it with the sandbox and the dialogue where learners state reasoning in their own words.
The reference triptych is a glossary/scaffold: it names mechanisms and examples but cannot show motion or rate response, so it should not be the first or only encounter.
Insulators slow energy transfer and do not generate heat (a blanket or duvet around ice keeps it cold); keep this explicit when discussing coats, wool and duvets.
Radiation is universal and not inherently nuclear or harmful: all objects emit and absorb infrared at all times.

The 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle and the metal-feels-colder 'feel' panel are idealised models: a real classroom cannot make a perfect vacuum, and metal only feels colder when it is cooler than the hand (a hotter-than-hand metal surface feels hot) — keep these qualifications visible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The IOP Spark source backing the misconception claims is marked verified:false in the row, and is the only backing for the misconception-targeting rationale; treat the efficacy framing (including the sourceClaims attached to activities 1, 2 and 4) as informed but not independently confirmed here.

Self-audit of science content: energy transfers from hotter to cooler (not 'cold flowing in'); in convection the less-dense heated fluid rises and carries energy (heat has no inherent upward direction); metal feels colder than wood at equal temperature because it conducts energy from the hand faster, not because it is a 'cold material', and when the metal is hotter than the hand it feels hot for the same fast-conduction reason.

Claims that a static image or 3D view 'cannot teach' / 'adds nothing' were rewritten as narrowly scoped affordance statements: a fixed diagram can teach vocabulary and canonical pictures but cannot be manipulated to show motion or rate response; a spatial view aids the genuinely 3D loop/spread but is not required.
The 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle is an idealised model; present it as demonstrating that no medium is needed, not as a literal achievable classroom vacuum.

The hot-railing counterexample, the duvet/insulator probe, the Leslie cube surface comparison, and the predict-then-measure thermometer reveal were drawn from the source assessment/representations into the activities to preserve those concrete examples; whether to use the hot-railing as core or extension is left to the teacher for this Tier B cohort.

assess.poeTask: Put out a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have shared the same room. Ask the child to predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) will read on each — different or the same — AND why. The 'metal is colder' child predicts a lower reading on the metal; the conduction child predicts equal readings. Then measure both to reveal they are identical.
probeDeeper: Predict the thermometer reading on each spoon before you measure. What do you expect, and why?
Counterexample: on a hot day (hotter than your body) a metal railing feels HOT, not cold. Why does the same 'good conductor' now feel hot?
Why does a duvet keep you warm if it doesn't produce any heat itself?
A radiator heats a room. Trace how conduction, convection and radiation each play a part.
assess.correctAnswer: No — both are at the same room temperature. The metal feels colder because it's a good conductor: it conducts heat away from your warm hand quickly, so your hand cools fast and feels the loss. Wood is a poor conductor, so it draws heat from your hand slowly and feels warmer. Feeling is about the RATE heat leaves your hand, not the object's temperature.

errorPatterns.pattern: Metal is naturally colder than wood, or metal 'holds/attracts cold' ('metal is a cold material').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure both with a thermometer — same temperature; reframe the feeling as heat leaving the hand fast through a good conductor.
errorPatterns.distractor: The metal spoon really is colder than the wooden one, because metal is a cold material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the two objects are at different temperatures, or that metal contains cold.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cold flows INTO the hand from the metal ('the cold moves into you') — cold as a transferred substance.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only energy (heat) moves, always hot→cold; 'cold' isn't a thing that flows — your hand loses heat to the metal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cold flows out of the metal and into your hand, which is why it feels cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes cold travelling into the hand rather than heat leaving it.

errorPatterns.pattern: In convection, heat itself rises ('heat rises') rather than hot fluid rising because it's less dense.
errorPatterns.nextMove: The heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks — it's the fluid that moves, carrying energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains a convection current as 'heat goes up', with no mention of density or fluid movement.

responseLevels.gap: Says the spoons are at different temperatures, or that cold flows into the hand; explains convection as 'heat rises' with no density.
responseLevels.full: Explains that feeling depends on the RATE heat leaves the hand (conduction), that only heat (not cold) is transferred hot→cold, convection as less-dense heated fluid rising, and that rate rises with temperature difference; handles the hot-railing counterexample.
responseLevels.partial: Explains metal conducts heat faster but still slips into 'cold flowing' language, or explains convection without density, or can't handle the hot-day counterexample.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have sat in the same room all day. The metal one feels colder to your hand. Are they actually at different temperatures? Explain why the metal feels colder even though both have been in the same room.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks metal is 'naturally colder' or 'holds cold' answers differently from one who explains the conduction rate from the hand. The reason tier separates 'metal is colder / attracts cold' from 'metal conducts heat away from my hand faster'.

sources.claim: KS3 Physics 'Energy: Energy changes and transfers' statutory wording covers heating and thermal equilibrium, energy transfer from hotter to cooler by contact (conduction) or radiation, transfers reducing the temperature difference, and use of insulators; convection is NOT explicitly named in this Energy statement (the particle-motion/spacing-with-temperature content sits under KS3 'Matter / Energy in matter').

sources.claim: NGSS MS-PS3-3 asks students [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3] minimizes or maximizes thermal energy transfer; DCI PS3.A states temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of matter, and PS3.B states energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions into colder ones.

Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
